clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive congenital cone dysfunction most often caused by mutations in CNGB3 or CNGA3, and less commonly GNAT2, PDE6C, or PDE6H
Presents in early infancy with pendular nystagmus, marked photophobia (day blindness), poor visual acuity, and absent or severely defective colour vision
The full-field electroretinogram shows absent or grossly reduced photopic (cone) responses with preserved scotopic (rod) responses
The fundus often appears near-normal in infancy, which can lead to delayed diagnosis despite abnormal function
Optical coherence tomography typically reveals disruption or loss of the foveal cone photoreceptor layer and outer retinal changes
Complete (typical) achromatopsia has total colour blindness, whereas incomplete forms retain some residual cone function and colour discrimination
Management is supportive with tinted or red-tinted lenses to reduce photophobia and low-vision aids, and it is a leading candidate condition for gene-replacement therapy trials
reference.pathophysiology: Achromatopsia arises from loss of function of the cone phototransduction cascade. Mutations most commonly affect the cyclic-nucleotide-gated channel subunits CNGB3 and CNGA3, and less often the cone transducin GNAT2 or phosphodiesterase subunits, disrupting the cones' ability to respond to light. Rod-mediated (scotopic) vision remains functional, so vision is relatively better in dim conditions, while bright light saturates the rods and produces disabling photophobia. Because central vision depends on the cone-rich fovea, cone dysfunction causes reduced acuity, nystagmus from lack of a stable foveal fixation signal, and impaired or absent colour perception. Progressive cone photoreceptor structural loss may occur at the fovea over time.
additionalDifferentials: Bilateral optic nerve or foveal hypoplasia
additionalInvestigations: Full-field electroretinography demonstrating absent cone with preserved rod responses
Detailed colour vision testing (e.g. Hardy-Rand-Rittler or arrangement tests)
Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the fovea
Molecular genetic testing (CNGB3, CNGA3 and related genes)
Assessment of best-corrected acuity and refraction under controlled lighting
redFlags: Nystagmus and photophobia in infancy requiring prompt paediatric ophthalmology and genetics referral
Progressive loss of foveal cone structure on imaging
Missed diagnosis attributed to a normal-looking fundus delaying appropriate support
reference.prognosis: Vision is stable in most patients with typically low but non-progressive acuity, though photophobia and colour blindness persist lifelong; the condition is generally non-degenerative, and emerging gene therapies offer future therapeutic promise.
pitfalls: Attributing infantile nystagmus and poor vision to a normal fundus and missing the electrophysiological diagnosis
Confusing achromatopsia with albinism or Leber congenital amaurosis
Overlooking the photophobia burden and failing to prescribe appropriate tinted lenses
Assuming complete colour blindness in all cases when incomplete forms retain partial function
management: Manage the disabling photophobia with dark or red-tinted filters and contact lenses, photochromic lenses and control of ambient lighting
Refractive correction and low-vision aids such as magnifiers, large print and high-contrast materials to optimise best-corrected acuity
Educational support and registration as sight-impaired where appropriate, with advice that driving is precluded
Regular ophthalmological and optical coherence tomography monitoring for any progressive foveal cone loss
Molecular genetic confirmation and genetic counselling for the autosomal recessive inheritance
Discuss emerging gene therapy directed at CNGB3 or CNGA3 and relevant clinical-trial options within a paediatric and low-vision service
